title: Sudden breathlessness in a 23-year-old man playing soccer
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 23-year-old engineering student who comes to the ED with sudden breathlessness and left-sided pleuritic chest pain that started during social soccer. The candidate then interprets his observations, ECG and chest X-ray, which shows a large left pneumothorax with no tension. They give a justified differential diagnosis, outline ED management of a symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax, and safety-net, including advice on recurrence, smoking, flying and diving.
focus: Acute breathlessness in a young adult: eliciting the features and risk factors of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax, excluding tension and the dangerous differentials, reading the chest X-ray, and managing a symptomatic pneumothorax
stem: You are a fourth-year medical student on your Emergency Department rotation at a metropolitan hospital. It is early evening. Chris Hamilton, a 23-year-old man, has come in with shortness of breath. He is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor. The consultant has asked you to see him. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations and recorded an ECG, and a chest X-ray has been requested.
tasks: Take a focused history from Chris and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, ECG and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Chris Hamilton, a 23-year-old university engineering student. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting up on the trolley, still in your soccer gear. You breathe fast and speak in short sentences, stopping between them to catch your breath. You are anxious. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Chris walked in about 20 minutes ago. At triage his resp rate was 24, sats 93% on room air, heart rate 106 and regular, BP 128/78, temp 36.8, pain 7 out of 10. The repeat a few minutes ago was resp rate 26, sats 93%, heart rate 110, BP 124/76. He's on the monitor, the ECG is done and the chest X-ray has been requested."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks, "What saturation are you aiming for?" With oxygen your sats come up to about 96%, but you are still short of breath.
  • If they offer pain relief and the nurse gives it, the pain eases to about 4/10 over 10 minutes and talking is a little easier.
  • If they ask you to lie flat, you say, "I'd rather sit up, it's harder to breathe lying down."
  • If they explain calmly what they are doing, you settle a little. If they use jargon, ask what it means.
  • If they ask for the X-ray or any results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I just... can't seem to... catch my breath."

History (give only when asked; short sentences):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: it came on suddenly this afternoon at about 3 pm while you were playing social soccer.
  • Injury: only if asked: no knock, tackle or fall onto your chest during the game.
  • Character: "I can't take a full breath."
  • Time course: it started about 2 hours ago and has been slowly getting worse. You have never had anything like this before.
  • What makes it better or worse: you sat out and rested, but it did not help. Any effort makes it worse.
  • Severity: you are breathless even sitting still. You can talk in short sentences but have to stop to catch your breath.

Chest pain (only if the candidate asks about chest pain)

  • Pain on the left side of your chest, sharp and worse when you breathe in. 7/10.
  • It started at the same time as the breathlessness.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all of these are no)

  • No cough, no coughing up blood, no phlegm.
  • No pain or swelling in either leg. No recent long trips, flights or time laid up in bed.
  • No wheeze, no chest tightness. No recent cold or flu.
  • No fever or shivers. No sick contacts.
  • No sweating apart from the soccer, no nausea, not pale. The pain is not crushing or central.
  • No palpitations. No dizziness, light-headedness or fainting. No unusual tiredness before today.

Past medical history

  • Wisdom teeth out at 18, no problems.
  • No known medical conditions. No asthma, no lung problems, no previous collapsed lung.
  • No connective tissue disorder such as Marfan syndrome (only if asked).
  • Only if asked: you are 185 cm tall and weigh 80 kg.

Medications

  • No prescription medicines.
  • Panadol occasionally.
  • Protein powder. Sometimes vitamins for your skin (B12 and zinc).
  • Recreational drugs: you have tried marijuana once.

Allergies: you think you are allergic to dogs (runny nose and sneezing). Nothing else, and no medicine allergies.

Family history

  • Mother, 58, well; had her gallbladder removed at 55.
  • Father, 60, well; has had a few skin cancers (BCCs) removed.
  • You are an only child.
  • No one in the family has had a collapsed lung or a connective tissue disorder (only if asked).

Social history

  • Smoking: you have smoked since you were 18, about 5 cigarettes a day.
  • Alcohol: socially, about 6 drinks each weekend.
  • Work and study: university engineering student; part-time school tutor.
  • Exercise: social soccer once a week; you walk to university most days.
  • Diet: relatively healthy.
  • Living: a share house with 2 other students.
  • Support: your family live in the same city and you see them monthly. You are close to your housemates and friends.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you have no idea what this is. At first you thought you were just out of breath from running, but it carried on after you rested. You had to stop playing and leave, and you feel you let the team down. You are worried because you are normally very healthy and cannot think what could cause this. You want to know what is going on and to be able to breathe properly.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "I'm normally really healthy. What could cause this?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: tall young man sitting upright, anxious. Breathing fast and using his neck muscles a little. Speaking in short sentences. Not cyanosed, not pale, not sweaty.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing. Mild nicotine staining of the right fingers.
  • Marfanoid features (if looked for): none. Arm span not greater than height, no high-arched palate, no joint hypermobility, no chest wall deformity.
  • Pulse: 110/min, regular, good volume.
  • Blood pressure: 124/76.
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Trachea: central.
  • Chest inspection: no bruising, wounds or deformity. Less movement on the left.
  • Palpation: chest wall not tender. Expansion reduced on the left. Apex beat in the normal position. No surgical emphysema.
  • Percussion: hyper-resonant over the left chest; resonant on the right.
  • Auscultation: markedly reduced breath sounds over the left chest, with reduced vocal resonance. Right side: vesicular breath sounds. No wheeze, no crackles, no pleural rub.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no pericardial rub.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender, no swelling.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Chris's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Acknowledges that he is breathless and anxious: keeps him sitting upright on the monitor, offers analgesia early, and keeps questions short and mostly closed.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when onset and at least 2 of the other 3 are elicited.

kids.x: Onset: sudden, at about 3 pm while playing soccer; no chest trauma
Character: cannot take a full breath
Time course: 2 hours, slowly worsening, first ever episode
Modifiers and severity: rest did not help, worse with any exertion, present at rest, speaking in short sentences

check.x: Asks about chest pain and elicits left-sided pleuritic pain, 7/10, which began at the same time as the breathlessness.
Asks about symptoms of the differentials:
check.d: Credit when at least 3 differentials are each explored with at least 3 relevant symptoms (source marking: full marks for 3 symptoms of 3 or more differentials).

kids.x: PE: cough, haemoptysis, pain or swelling in one leg, recent long-distance travel or immobilisation
Asthma: wheeze, cough, chest tightness, history of asthma or atopy, recent URTI
ACS: central crushing chest pain, sweating, nausea, pallor
Arrhythmia: palpitations, fatigue, dizziness or loss of consciousness
Viral pericarditis: fever, recent sick contacts, sharp chest pain, palpitations

check.x: Asks about pneumothorax risk factors: previous pneumothorax, connective tissue disorder (Marfan), underlying lung disease such as asthma, and family history of pneumothorax (all absent).
Takes the past medical history: wisdom teeth removed at 18, no medical conditions; notes he is tall (185 cm, 80 kg).
Takes the medication and allergy history: no prescription medicines, occasional Panadol, protein powder, B12 and zinc; marijuana once; allergic to dogs only, no medicine allergies.
Takes a family history: mother 58 and well (cholecystectomy at 55), father 60 and well (BCCs removed), only child.
Quantifies smoking: about 5 cigarettes a day since 18 (about 1.25 pack-years), current smoker.

Takes the rest of the social history: about 6 drinks each weekend, engineering student and part-time tutor, weekly soccer and walking, share house with 2 students, family in the same city and close friends.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 of these are covered.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thought he was just out of breath from running, feels he let the team down, worried because he is normally healthy and has no idea of the cause.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: distress, speech in short sentences, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, tall body habitus, and the nurse's observations (RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air, HR 110).
Respiratory examination identifying a left pneumothorax:
check.d: Credit when percussion and auscultation are both performed and compared side to side.

kids.x: Reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance on the left
Right side normal; no wheeze, crackles or rub

check.x: Looks specifically for signs of tension and states they are absent: trachea central, BP maintained, JVP not raised, apex beat not displaced, warm peripheries.
Completes the cardiovascular and leg examination: pulse rhythm, heart sounds with no rub, and soft non-tender calves (against DVT).
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone with RR and HR rising, needing clinical review; HR white but tachycardic; BP normal, so not haemodynamically compromised.
Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic ST change, no pericarditis pattern and no arrhythmia, arguing against ACS, pericarditis and arrhythmia.
Reads the chest X-ray:
check.d: Credit when the pleural line, the absent lung markings and the absence of mediastinal shift are all stated.

kids.x: Patient details, date and view (erect AP)
A clearly visible left visceral pleural line
No lung markings beyond the pleural line
No mediastinal shift or diaphragm depression, so no radiological tension
Large: 3 cm interpleural distance at the hilum (2 cm or more); right lung clear

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as a left primary spontaneous pneumothorax without tension, justified by a tall young male smoker with sudden breathlessness and left pleuritic pain, left hyper-resonance with reduced breath sounds, and the X-ray.

Names differentials with a relative negative for each: PE (no leg swelling, travel or haemoptysis), asthma (no wheeze or asthma history), ACS (age 23, pleuritic pain, normal ECG), and pericarditis or pneumonia.
check.d: Credit when at least 3 differentials are named, each with a feature from this patient.

check.x: Management
Escalates to the senior ED doctor or ED registrar, with continuous monitoring, regular observations, IV access and the patient sitting upright.
Gives oxygen if SpO2 falls below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96% (TSANZ), and analgesia: regular paracetamol 1 g, plus titrated opioid if needed.

States that intervention is needed because he is significantly symptomatic (breathless at rest) with a large pneumothorax: needle aspiration by an experienced clinician, a repeat chest X-ray afterwards, and a small-bore chest drain to an underwater seal with admission if aspiration fails.
check.d: Credit an ambulatory pneumothorax device as an alternative to aspiration.

check.x: States that if he develops signs of tension (hypotension, rising heart rate, falling SpO2, tracheal deviation), he needs immediate needle or finger decompression without waiting for an X-ray, followed by a chest drain.

Plans disposition: discharge with written advice if the lung re-expands and symptoms settle; otherwise admit under the respiratory team, with a thoracic surgical referral for a persistent air leak or failure to re-expand.

Explains in plain words that air has leaked from a small weak spot on the surface of the left lung and partly collapsed it, that this is a known problem in tall young men, especially smokers, and that it is not caused by anything he did in the game. Checks understanding.
Advises stopping smoking because it raises the risk of it happening again, and offers support (NRT, Quitline).
Safety netting
Tells Chris in plain words to come straight back to ED, or call 000, if he becomes more short of breath, has new or worse chest pain, feels faint or dizzy, or his heart races.

Gives activity advice: no flying until an X-ray confirms the lung has fully re-expanded; avoid scuba diving permanently unless he has definitive surgery; no contact sport or heavy exertion until cleared at follow-up.
Arranges follow-up: respiratory clinic review with a repeat chest X-ray in about 2 to 4 weeks, a letter to his GP, and tells him the risk of recurrence (about 1 in 3).

part2.lead: Here are his observations, the ECG the nurse recorded and the chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4, one at a time:

  • "Was it something I did in the game?"
  • "Will it happen again? When can I play soccer again?"

You are relieved to have an explanation. If the candidate explains clearly, you accept the plan. If they mention smoking, say: "I only have a few a day. Does that really matter?" If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets taken on room air before any treatment; the 17:10 set was taken just before you arrived.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 24 and SpO2 93% on room air are in the yellow zone; HR 106, BP 128/78 and temperature 36.8 °C are white; pain 7/10. At 17:10 RR has risen to 26 (yellow), SpO2 stays 93% (yellow), HR has risen to 110 (white) and BP is 124/76.
  • Meaning: tachypnoea, mild hypoxia and tachycardia, worsening slightly, with a normal BP: a symptomatic pneumothorax with no haemodynamic compromise. A white-zone heart rate does not mean he is safe.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior review now with repeat observations. Oxygen if SpO2 falls below 92%. Any red-zone value (SBP below 90, HR 140 or more, SpO2 in the red zone, RR 30 or more) calls for a rapid response and immediate reassessment for tension.

rows.note: Triage: to acute bay, monitor on, ECG requested
Repeat set at bedside before medical review

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mr Chris Hamilton, age 23, recorded at 17:00 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 108/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +70°.
  • PR interval: 140 ms. No PR depression. No delta wave.
  • QRS duration: 86 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 410 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression in any lead. T waves upright apart from aVR.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves. No S1Q3T3 pattern. Normal R wave progression.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 108/min, normal axis and intervals. No ST or T wave change, no PR depression, no pre-excitation and no arrhythmia.
  • Meaning: sinus tachycardia fits pain, breathlessness and hypoxia from the pneumothorax. There is no ischaemia (against ACS), no widespread ST elevation or PR depression (against pericarditis) and no arrhythmia to explain his symptoms. A normal ECG does not exclude PE.
  • Changes: no cardiac pathway is needed; the work-up rests on the chest X-ray.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, erect AP view. Mr Chris Hamilton, 23, taken today at 17:25.

Clinical details: 23-year-old man, smoker, with sudden breathlessness and left pleuritic chest pain during soccer 2 hours ago. Reduced breath sounds on the left. SpO2 93% on room air.

Findings:

  • Technical: erect AP film, adequate inspiration, not rotated, adequate penetration.
  • Pleura: a thin, sharp visceral pleural line is seen on the left, running parallel to the chest wall from the apex down the lateral chest wall. No lung markings are visible beyond it. The interpleural distance at the level of the hilum is 3 cm. No fluid level. Right pleura normal.
  • Lungs: the left lung is partly collapsed towards the hilum, with no consolidation. No bullae are seen. The right lung is clear.
  • Heart and mediastinum: trachea and mediastinum central, with no shift to the right. Heart size normal.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms in a normal position; the left is not depressed or flattened. Costophrenic angles clear.
  • Bones and soft tissues: rib spacing symmetrical. No rib fracture. No surgical emphysema.

Conclusion: large left pneumothorax (interpleural distance 3 cm at the hilum). No radiological features of tension.
handover.model:
• Read: confirms the name, date and an erect AP film, adequate quality. The obvious abnormality first: a visible left visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. Then systematically: interpleural distance 3 cm at the hilum, so a large pneumothorax (2 cm or more, BTS); no mediastinal shift, no depressed hemidiaphragm, symmetrical rib spacing; right lung clear; no fracture, fluid level or surgical emphysema.
  • Meaning: a large left primary spontaneous pneumothorax without tension, matching the left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds. No rib fracture or underlying lung disease is seen.
  • Changes: he is symptomatic at rest, so he needs an intervention (needle aspiration or an ambulatory device, with a small-bore drain if that fails) and a repeat film afterwards. No D-dimer or troponin is needed now that the cause is clear.

ask: You are now calling the emergency registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Chris Hamilton, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Chris now, here in the emergency department.
Before Chris goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student in ED; Chris Hamilton, 23.
  • Situation: large left pneumothorax, no tension; RR 26 and SpO2 93% on room air (yellow zone), HR 110, BP 124/76.
  • Background: sudden breathlessness and left pleuritic pain 7/10 at 3 pm playing soccer, no trauma, first episode; smoker about 5 a day since 18; no lung disease or connective tissue disorder; no regular medicines; no medicine allergies.
  • Assessment: left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, trachea central; ECG sinus tachycardia only; CXR left pleural line, no markings beyond, 3 cm at the hilum, no mediastinal shift. Symptomatic large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, stable.
  • Recommendation: please review now for needle aspiration; analgesia started, monitoring and repeat observations.

Left primary spontaneous pneumothorax, no tension: tall young male smoker; sudden breathlessness and left pleuritic pain on exertion, worsening over 2 hours; left reduced expansion, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds; CXR pleural line with absent markings.

  • Tension pneumothorax: must be excluded; against: BP normal, trachea central, no mediastinal shift.
  • PE: for: sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, smoker; against: no leg swelling, travel, immobility or haemoptysis; CXR explains it.
  • Asthma: for: dog allergy; against: no wheeze, no asthma history, unilateral hyper-resonance.
  • ACS: against: age 23, pleuritic not crushing pain, normal ECG.
  • Pericarditis: against: no viral illness or fever, no rub, normal ECG.

1. Senior ED review; continuous monitoring; sit upright; IV access.
  2. Oxygen if SpO2 below 92%, target 92 to 96%. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g regularly (maximum 4 g a day), titrated IV opioid if needed.
  3. Symptomatic and large, so intervene: needle aspiration (or an ambulatory device) by an experienced clinician; stop if more than 2.5 L is aspirated.
  4. Repeat chest X-ray. If re-expanded and symptoms settle: discharge with advice. If aspiration fails: small-bore chest drain to an underwater seal and admit under respiratory.
  5. Tension (hypotension, rising HR, falling SpO2, tracheal deviation): immediate decompression, no X-ray first, then a chest drain.
  6. Thoracic surgical referral for a persistent air leak or failure to re-expand.
  7. Smoking cessation: NRT, Quitline.

• Explanation: a small weak spot on the lung surface leaked air; not caused by the game.
  • Red flags (ED or 000): more breathless, new or worse chest pain, faint or dizzy, racing heart.
  • Recurrence: about 1 in 3; stopping smoking lowers it (Quitline, NRT).
  • Activity: no flying until an X-ray shows the lung fully re-expanded; no scuba diving unless he has definitive surgery; no soccer or heavy exertion until cleared at follow-up.
  • Follow-up: respiratory clinic with a repeat chest X-ray in about 2 to 4 weeks; letter to his GP; written information.

ddx.dx: Left primary spontaneous pneumothorax without tension
ddx.for: A tall 23-year-old male smoker with sudden breathlessness and left pleuritic pain during soccer, left hyper-resonance with reduced breath sounds, and a left pleural line with absent lung markings on X-ray.
Large left pneumothorax with tachycardia, tachypnoea and a slowly worsening course.
ddx.against: BP is normal, the trachea is central, the JVP is not raised and the X-ray shows no mediastinal shift.

ddx.for: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness with tachycardia and mild hypoxia in a smoker.
ddx.against: No leg pain or swelling, travel, immobilisation or haemoptysis, and the X-ray explains his symptoms.

ddx.for: Breathlessness on exertion and a possible atopic history (dog allergy).
ddx.against: No wheeze, cough, chest tightness or asthma history, and the chest signs are on one side only.

ddx.for: Chest pain and breathlessness in a smoker during exertion.
ddx.against: He is 23 with pleuritic rather than central crushing pain, no sweating or nausea, and a normal ECG apart from sinus tachycardia.

ddx.for: Sharp chest pain worse on breathing in, with tachycardia.
ddx.against: No fever, recent viral illness or sick contacts, no pericardial rub, and no widespread ST elevation or PR depression on the ECG.

guide:
In Part 1, Chris answers in short, breathless sentences, and the nurse gives the opening observations. He mentions the chest pain only if the candidate asks about pain. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for the X-ray or other results in Part 1, say these will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Chris asks his questions after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate characterises the sudden breathlessness, asks about chest pain and finds the left pleuritic pain. They screen at least three differentials with targeted symptoms, ask about pneumothorax risk factors and quantify his smoking. They compare percussion and breath sounds side to side and actively look for signs of tension. In Part 2 they read the X-ray by stating the pleural line first, then systematically, and note the absence of mediastinal shift. They recognise that a large pneumothorax in a patient breathless at rest needs intervention, know what to do if tension develops, and give specific advice about smoking, flying and diving.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history, misses the chest pain or the smoking, and does not percuss. They may call the X-ray normal or miss the pleural line, or may not comment on tension. Waiting for an X-ray before decompressing a patient with clinical tension, or sending Chris home without advice about flying, diving and when to return, is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: left primary spontaneous pneumothorax

A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space, between the visceral and parietal pleura. A primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) happens without known lung disease, usually from rupture of small apical blebs or bullae. A secondary pneumothorax happens with underlying lung disease such as COPD, asthma or cystic fibrosis. PSP is common in the early 20s and rare after 40. It typically affects young, tall, thin men, and smoking is a major risk factor. Chris fits this picture: a tall 23-year-old male smoker with sudden breathlessness and left pleuritic chest pain that started during exercise and did not settle with rest.

The history

  • Breathlessness: sudden onset, what he was doing (and whether there was chest trauma), the course, modifiers and severity (breathless at rest, speaking in short sentences).
  • Chest pain: pleuritic pain on the affected side usually starts with the breathlessness. Ask about it directly.
  • Risk factors: smoking, tall stature, previous pneumothorax, family history, connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos) and lung disease.
  • Differentials: PE (haemoptysis, leg swelling, travel, immobilisation), asthma (wheeze, tightness, atopy, URTI), pneumonia (productive cough, fever), ACS (central crushing pain, sweating, nausea, pallor), arrhythmia (palpitations, dizziness, syncope) and viral pericarditis (fever, sick contacts, sharp pain).

The examination

A small pneumothorax may give a normal examination. A large one gives reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, and reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance on the affected side. Accessory muscle use suggests a sizeable pneumothorax. Tension adds tachycardia, hypotension, a raised JVP and, late, tracheal deviation away from the affected side. Tension is a clinical diagnosis: it is treated at once by decompression, not after an X-ray.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone call for a clinical review. A normal BP shows he is not haemodynamically compromised. Any red-zone value calls for a rapid response and a check for tension.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia, with no ischaemia, pericarditis pattern or arrhythmia.
  • Chest X-ray: if short of time, state the obvious abnormality first (the pleural line), then go through RIPE (rotation, inspiration, projection, exposure) and ABCDEF (airway, breathing, cardiac, diaphragm, everything else, foreign bodies or lines). A pneumothorax shows a thin white visceral pleural line, with no lung markings beyond it. Tension adds a larger pneumothorax, wider rib spacing, contralateral mediastinal shift and a depressed hemidiaphragm. Chris has a large pneumothorax (interpleural distance 2 cm or more at the hilum, BTS) with no features of tension. Beware skin folds, which can mimic a pleural line. On a supine film, air collects anteriorly and may show only as a deep sulcus sign. CT helps when the X-ray is uncertain.
  • Other tests: FBE may show a mild leukocytosis, and an arterial gas shows hypoxaemia. D-dimer and troponin are considered only when the diagnosis is uncertain and other differentials need excluding.

Management of a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax

  1. Resuscitate and escalate: airway, breathing, circulation, monitoring and senior help. If tension is suspected, decompress immediately (needle or finger thoracostomy), then insert a chest drain.
  2. Oxygen if hypoxaemic, titrated to SpO2 92 to 96% (TSANZ). Analgesia: paracetamol, with a titrated opioid if needed.
  3. Choose by symptoms (the BTS 2023 guideline puts symptoms ahead of size):
    • Minimal symptoms: conservative management (observation, then outpatient review) is an option. The Australian and New Zealand PSP trial found conservative management non-inferior to intervention for moderate to large PSP in selected patients.
    • Significant symptoms (breathless at rest, as Chris is): needle aspiration, or an ambulatory pneumothorax device where available. Stop aspirating if more than 2.5 L is removed. Repeat the chest X-ray afterwards.
    • If aspiration fails: a small-bore chest drain (Seldinger) to an underwater seal, with admission under the respiratory team.
  4. Surgery: refer to thoracic surgery for a persistent air leak or failure to re-expand, a second ipsilateral pneumothorax, a contralateral pneumothorax, and people in high-risk occupations such as pilots and divers.

Safety netting and follow-up

Chris needs to come straight back to ED, or call 000, if he gets more short of breath, has new or worse chest pain, feels faint or has a racing heart. About a third of people have a recurrence, and stopping smoking reduces the risk, so offer NRT and Quitline. He should not fly until an X-ray confirms full re-expansion, and should avoid scuba diving permanently unless he has definitive surgery. He should not play contact sport or do heavy exertion until he is cleared at follow-up. Arrange a respiratory clinic review with a repeat chest X-ray in about 2 to 4 weeks, written information, and a letter to his GP.
points: Think of primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a tall young smoker with sudden breathlessness and one-sided pleuritic pain, and ask about chest pain directly: patients often mention only the breathlessness.
Compare percussion and breath sounds side to side: hyper-resonance with reduced breath sounds on one side is a pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
Tension is a clinical diagnosis (hypotension, tachycardia, raised JVP, late tracheal deviation) and is decompressed immediately, never after waiting for an X-ray.
On the chest X-ray, state the pleural line first, then confirm absent lung markings beyond it, measure the size (2 cm or more at the hilum is large) and look for mediastinal shift.
Manage by symptoms: minimal symptoms can be observed; a breathless patient needs needle aspiration or an ambulatory device, with a small-bore drain if that fails.
Safety-net about recurrence (about 1 in 3), stopping smoking, no flying until X-ray resolution, no scuba diving without definitive surgery, and respiratory follow-up with a repeat X-ray.
